Europe Spent €16.5 Million Proving Again That Hydrogen Burns in a Turbine

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that hydrogen burns.
  • The latest Siemens Energy announcement, dated November 16, 2026, describes an SGT-400 turbine at Smurfit Westrock’s Saillat-sur-Vienne paper mill operating on pure hydrogen through startup, load changes and full-load cogeneration.
  • In a recent development, siemens’ own March 2024 technical article supplied the most important numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hydrogen burns. Turbines spin. Their exhaust can make steam. Kawasaki demonstrated hydrogen-fired electricity and heat production at Kobe Port Island in 2018, before Europe funded the first HYFLEXPOWER programme. Six years later, Siemens Energy is still issuing announcements about hydrogen combustion at a single turbine in a French paper mill. European and British taxpayers have supplied roughly €16.5 million for the two research programmes, and the same installation has generated at least 78 identified press appearances. Neither the grants nor the publicity have produced a commercial reason to make hydrogen from electricity and burn it for industrial electricity and steam.

The latest Siemens Energy announcement, dated November 16, 2026, describes an SGT-400 turbine at Smurfit Westrock’s Saillat-sur-Vienne paper mill operating on pure hydrogen through startup, load changes and full-load cogeneration. The equipment can operate under those conditions. Hydrogen combustion and heat recovery were already established. Extending the operating range of one manufacturer’s turbine has not changed hydrogen’s production cost, the losses involved in making it or the available alternatives. No second commercial installation has emerged from the programme.

In a recent development, siemens’ own March 2024 technical article supplied the most important numbers. The electrolyzer installed at the paper mill produces 16.4 kg of hydrogen per hour. The turbine consumes about 810 kg per hour when producing 10 MW of electricity. Onsite production covers 2.02% of hourly fuel demand. Nearly 50 times that electrolyzer capacity would be needed to supply the turbine continuously at the stated operating point. Later testing used hydrogen brought to the site.

In a recent development, the 2023 campaign accumulated about 90 hours of hydrogen and natural-gas blending tests, including just over four hours on pure hydrogen. Siemens identified limited hydrogen availability as the constraint. The 2026 announcement supplies no cumulative full-load hydrogen operating hours, delivered fuel price or routine cost of electricity and steam. These are the figures an industrial customer needs before buying equipment. Announcing another combustion test avoids the question of who will supply hundreds of kilograms of affordable hydrogen every hour for years.

My complete TFIE Strategy Briefing investigation examines the funding records, Siemens’ published operating figures, the energy balance and an audited chronology of 78 press appearances surrounding the same turbine.

According to recent reports, at an illustrative 50 kWh of electricity per kilogram of hydrogen, manufacturing the turbine’s 810 kg of hourly fuel requires approximately 40.5 MW of electricity. The turbine returns about 10 MW of electricity plus usable exhaust heat. Compression, storage and delivery add equipment and expense. The mill needs electricity and process steam; converting electricity into gas and burning it to recover those services introduces losses and costs that direct electrification avoids.

According to recent reports, france is an especially poor location for this detour. RTE’s 2025 electricity review reports that 95.2% of French generation was low-carbon, with average generation emissions of 19.6 gCO₂e/kWh. Direct grid power can supply the electrical load. Industrial heat pumps, mechanical vapour recompression, electric boilers and thermal storage can supply process heat and steam in combinations designed around the mill’s operating requirements. The programme should have compared these complete systems before committing public money to more hydrogen turbine retrofits.

A paper mill in Finland is already doing the industrial work. Delfort’s Tervakoski plant has operated a Turboden heat pump and mechanical vapour-recompression installation since January 2026. It supplies about 12 MW of process steam at temperatures up to 170°C, with a reported coefficient of performance around two. It delivers useful steam without a hydrogen-production plant, hydrogen deliveries or a hydrogen-fired turbine. The exact plant integration will vary, but the alternative is operating commercially while HyCoFlex continues issuing test announcements.

According to recent reports, the funding was directed at the wrong problem. HYFLEXPOWER received €10.48 million in EU support. HyCoFlex received another €4.44 million. A Siemens presentation identifies approximately €1.56 million more in UK support, bringing the public contribution across the programmes to about €16.48 million. Both programmes were designed around making existing gas-turbine cogeneration equipment compatible with hydrogen. The grants paid for additional turbine operating conditions instead of establishing that hydrogen was a sensible way to provide the plant’s energy.

It has been revealed that the programme’s economics were weak before the second award. In October 2023, Siemens presented a scenario requiring electricity below €35/MWh to bring hydrogen fuel costs into parity with natural gas under its 2022 cost assumptions. The HYFLEXPOWER final workshop later examined favourable operating cases with hydrogen substitution and electrolyzer utilization both above 90%. European reporting also identified renewable electricity below €40/MWh as a condition for favourable deployment economics. France’s 2025 wholesale electricity averaged €61.1/MWh. Its negative-price hours were occasional. They could not supply a plant operating more than 90% of the time. These conditions were set out before the research programme ended, yet funding continued for more combustion trials.

Recent findings suggest that siemens also has a clear commercial interest in preserving turbine markets. Its 2025 presentation explicitly described protecting existing assets and future gas-turbine investments in a decarbonizing world as a benefit of hydrogen compatibility. A turbine supplier is entitled to pursue its products with its own money. The purpose of public industrial-decarbonization funding is to reduce emissions and costs, not to protect combustion-equipment sales from direct-electric competition.

The TFIE media audit counted 19 press appearances in 2020, 13 in the 2022 installation and blending phase, 35 around the 2023 tests and award, four in 2024 and seven through November 16, 2026. Those 78 appearances trace back to a handful of announcements about one installation. They are not 78 independent engineering advances or 78 deployments. The headline count swelled while the operating fleet did not.

Public funders should require equipment-neutral comparisons of delivered industrial energy services before underwriting another hydrogen retrofit. The evidence needed is familiar: a year’s reliable electricity and steam, actual operating cost, lifecycle emissions, fuel contracts, and performance against direct-electric alternatives. HyCoFlex has supplied more hydrogen-combustion publicity without establishing those outcomes. The problem was not that Europe failed to make a turbine burn hydrogen. It was that public money kept flowing after the relevant energy and economic questions already had answers.

It has been revealed that the full TFIE Strategy Briefing investigation contains the audited funding and media evidence, the 2% onsite hydrogen-supply calculation and the direct-electric industrial steam comparison. TFIE Strategy provides evidence-based assessments of industrial energy investments and public programmes.

  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned in September that Iran would have "nothing left to trade" within two weeks.
  • Nearly two months later, the Trump administration is still targeting the overseas financial networks Tehran has used to keep money moving despite sweeping U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent joins 'Sunday Morning Futures' to discuss the Trump administration's economic sanctions against Iran, predicting a swift collapse of the regime's economy. Bessent also addresses the Iranian death threats that forced his family to relocate to a military base and weighs in on the compliance failures at Nvidia amid its ongoing espionage probe.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned in September that Iran would have "nothing left to trade" within two weeks.

Nearly two months later, the Trump administration is still targeting the overseas financial networks Tehran has used to keep money moving despite sweeping U.S. sanctions in the midst of ongoing war.

On Monday, Treasury confirmed another round of sanctions targeting more than two dozen individuals and companies accused of helping Iran move billions of dollars through financial networks spanning Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey.

Sources indicate that bessent has repeatedly warned that Iran is nearing economic collapse, describing successive crackdowns as steps toward cutting off the regime's remaining financial lifelines. Yet each upcoming round of sanctions has exposed more of the networks Tehran has used to keep doing business abroad — even as mounting economic pressure has failed to produce a diplomatic breakthrough.

COULD IRAN’S REGIME COLLAPSE? EXPERTS ASSESS BESSENT’S BID TO SEVER FINANCIAL LIFELINES.

It has been revealed that secretary Scott Bessent speaks to members of the media outside the White House in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 22, 2025 (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

While the administration claims its blockade has largely stopped Iranian oil exports, Monday's sanctions detail how Tehran has relied on currency dealers, trading companies and middlemen to conduct business abroad.

Treasury identified approximately $14.7 billion in financial activity potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking between January 2025 and August 2026, underscoring the scale of the networks Washington is now targeting.

It has been revealed that just three days earlier, Treasury declared that Iran had exhausted its seaborne oil supply outside the U.S. blockade, saying no fresh oil had been loaded onto vessels since the launch of Operation Economic Outcast in August.

In a recent development, "The regime has exhausted its seaborne oil supply, and it may never see the revenue from the oil it has already sold. The ship is sinking," Bessent stated Friday.

In a response to Fox News Digital, Treasury mentioned Iran has not loaded a single barrel of oil onto vessels since Aug. 25, 2026, and claimed Tehran is struggling to access foreign currency and recover proceeds from previous oil sales.

The department also provided a report showing the Iranian rial has lost roughly 25% of its value since August, while inflation reached 90% in September. Treasury noted it is continuing to target alternative financial channels, including cryptocurrency exchanges, as Tehran looks for ways around U.S. restrictions.

BESSENT NOTES IRAN WILL HAVE 'NOTHING LEFT TO TRADE' WITHIN TWO WEEKS AS OIL LIFELINE DRIES UP.

It has been revealed that A cargo ship sails in the Persian Gulf toward the Strait of Hormuz, April 22, 2026. (AP Photo).

But even as the administration claims success in cutting off newly introduced oil shipments, Treasury is still pursuing Iranian operatives accused of collecting billions of dollars from previous sales. Friday's sanctions targeted four individuals involved in recovering oil revenues held overseas, some of which Treasury remarked had been diverted by middlemen for personal gain.

Bessent's September prediction was hardly his first warning that Tehran was approaching an economic breaking point.

Months earlier, he remarked U.S. sanctions were "asphyxiating" Iran's economy and warned that the country could soon be forced to shut down oil wells as storage facilities filled up.

UPCOMING YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order.

It has been revealed that the companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order issued late Friday says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

According to recent reports, the order is the Republican administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets, noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon.

White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations initiated by Democrats.

Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality.".

It has been revealed that garcia sent letters this week directing members of Trump's family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.

Responding to the upcoming executive order, Garcia said it was part of the administration's "blatant attack on Congress' constitutional right to conduct oversight." He said that despite efforts to impede investigations, "we're just getting started.".

In a fact sheet, the White House framed the fresh requirements as "protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach," arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by "harassing private companies that contract with the federal government.".

Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.

The latest executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.

ICE’s intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable," Campbell remarked in a statement.

DOJ SUES TO STOP OHIO COURT BLOCKING COURTHOUSE ARRESTS.

In a recent development, massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration to block ICE agents from carrying out civil arrests in the state's courthouses. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images).

"ICE is misleading the public by suggesting that these arrests make us safer when, in fact, ICE's actions are preventing criminal cases from moving forward, denying a victim’s ability to obtain accountability, violating a defendant’s due process, and leaving open the possibility that someone facing serious criminal charges could ultimately be released from ICE custody without their criminal case ever being resolved," she continued.

The attorney general said more than 1,110 people have been arrested at her state's courthouses since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, including more than 600 people in 2025 and more than 500 during the first 10 months of 2026.

Campbell stated ICE has ignored the new state law and arrested at least 38 people in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants in the two and a half weeks since the courthouse protections went into effect.

"I, along with our district attorneys, share the goal of holding defendants accountable for crimes, yet ICE’s unlawful tactics to arrest someone for a civil immigration violation is not the same as holding them accountable for a crime," Campbell remarked.

FEDERAL JUDGE IN NEW YORK TIES TRUMP ADMIN HANDS ON ARRESTS AT IMMIGRATION COURTS.

Industry observers note that the attorney general noted more than 1,110 people have been arrested at her state's courthouses since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. (Getty Images).

Campbell noted that ICE's courthouse arrests have continued in Massachusetts despite a federal ruling handed down in June by U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in California that vacated the Trump administration's courthouse arrest policy ​in a separate class action lawsuit.

In Monday's lawsuit, Campbell argues the ICE policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act since it was adopted without taking into account the impact it would have on states and because the Immigration and Nationality Act does not explicitly authorize courthouse arrests.

The lawsuit also alleges that the ⁠policy violates the U.S. Constitution's Tenth Amendment, which protects states' rights to maintain authority over their own judicial systems.

"The Trump Administration’s ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses are interfering with our justice system and undermining public safety. When people are afraid to go to court, victims are less likely to report crimes, survivors are less likely to seek protection, and our communities are less safe," Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey stated in a statement. "We expect ICE and all federal agents to follow Massachusetts law.".

The lawsuit challenges a 2025 ICE directive that instructs agents to conduct civil arrests in or near state courthouses without judicial warrants. (Bloomberg via Getty Images).

  • The U.S.-Israel alliance was tested when Washington and Jerusalem found common cause against Iran — and when defending Israel drew heavily on American weapons stocks.
  • A new report from Advancing American Freedom (AAF) and the Zionist Organization of America (ZOA) argues that Israel’s military reach and regional role make the alliance a strategic asset for Washington.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed was confronted on NBC's "Meet the Press" Sunday over his opposition to Israel's existence as a Jewish state.

The U.S.-Israel alliance was tested when Washington and Jerusalem found common cause against Iran — and when defending Israel drew heavily on American weapons stocks. Meanwhile, that ongoing conflict has now sharpened a question for Washington: what does the alliance deliver, and what does it demand in return?

A new report from Advancing American Freedom (AAF) and the Zionist Organization of America (ZOA) argues that Israel’s military reach and regional role make the alliance a strategic asset for Washington.

Sources indicate that its authors call Israel "the largest U.S. aircraft carrier" in the Middle East. But this is in direct opposition of critics who say that the alliance costs the U.S. a lot and delivers very little in return.

The report, dated Oct. 26, 2026, arrives as public support for Israel continues to fall across the political spectrum — even among Republicans and MAGA supporters.

FROM INTELLIGENCE SHARING TO MISSILE DEFENSE, HOW ISRAEL'S PARTNERSHIP PROTECTS AMERICAN SECURITY.

President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed joint military action targeting Iran. (REUTERS/Kevin Mohatt).

President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have discussed ending direct U.S. military aid, but the U.S. leader has also called Israel "a great ally, much more reliable than most" and noted Washington would help if Israel needed it.

The report specifically points to intelligence sharing, joint weapons development and military cooperation as returns on what the U.S. gets for providing support to Israel.

It has been revealed that one of the clearest examples is missile defense. The U.S. and Israel develop systems including David’s Sling and Arrow, while American companies manufacture components for several programs. More than 100 companies across 34 states participate in missile-defense co-production, according to the Congressional Research Service. In August, a Raytheon-Rafael facility in Arkansas delivered the first Iron Dome Tamir interceptor built entirely in the U.S.

Those programs support U.S. manufacturers and give the Pentagon a role in developing missile-defense systems. During the Iran conflict, however, U.S. forces also expended large numbers of interceptors — costly weapons that can take years to replace.

US REBUILDING WEAPONS STOCKPILE COULD DELAY ORDERS FROM ALLIES.

Recent findings suggest that in September, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated that the U.S. had probably used between half and two-thirds of its combined inventory of Patriot, THAAD, SM-3 and SM-6 interceptors since June 2025.

The estimate includes weapons used during the earlier 12-day war with Iran and is based on publicly reported expenditures compared with the number of those interceptors the War Department has purchased. CBO said rebuilding stocks could take at least five years, even if production increased.

President Donald Trump, left, meets with Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, as CIA Director John Ratcliffe, from second left, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, and from second right, Netanyahu's wife Sara Netanyahu, Israel's Strategic Affairs Minister Ron Dermer, Israel's National Security Council head Tzachi Hanegbi, obstructed, and Israel's Cabinet Secretary Yossi Fuchs listen in the Blue Room of the White House, Monday, July 7, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon).

Intelligence sharing is another return cited by supporters of the alliance. Former CIA Director John Brennan stated Israeli intelligence was among the "thousands of bits" considered during the years-long effort to find Usama bin Laden. He did not specify what Israel provided or how much it contributed to the operation.

A more recent exchange shows how Israeli reporting can prompt U.S. action even when its accuracy is uncertain. Israeli officials warned the U.S. of a possible Iranian plot to kill Trump during a trip to Turkey. The Secret Service took precautions, including moving him to another aircraft. U.S. intelligence agencies could not independently verify the threat, however, and the CIA assessed some of the Israeli reporting with "low confidence," according to Reuters and The Washington Post.

NETANYAHU REVEALS HE WANTS AMERICAN FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL TO 'DRAW DOWN TO ZERO'.

In a recent development, the financial relationship has also become part of the debate. Under the current agreement, the U.S. provides Israel with $3.3 billion annually in Foreign Military Financing and $500 million for joint missile-defense programs. Most of the military aid pays for weapons and services from U.S. contractors, according to CRS. Israel’s ability to spend a portion of the funding on domestic purchases is scheduled to phase out by 2028.

In a recent development, the report's authors call the $3.8 billion in annual U.S. military aid "one of the highest returns on investment of any U.S. foreign assistance.".

Trump has stated he wants to end annual aid, while Netanyahu has also publicly called for phasing it out over time. U.S. and Israeli officials have been negotiating a latest agreement that could wind down direct assistance while expanding joint defense projects and weapons production. The current agreement runs through 2028, Congress controls appropriations, and no successor deal has been reached.

TRUMP WANTS LARGEST-EVER ISRAELI HEAVY BOMB TRANSFER — BUT PROPOSAL HAS CONGRESS PREPARING FOR $2.8B FIGHT.

According to recent reports, the Israeli Iron Dome air defense system fires to intercept missiles during an Iranian attack over Tel Aviv, Israel, early Wednesday, June 18, 2025. (AP Photo/Leo Correa).

The debate is also becoming more politically consequential as Americans question the relationship’s terms.

A 2026 Chicago Council survey found that 56% favored reducing or ending U.S. military aid to Israel. Republicans remain more supportive than Democrats and independents, but the right is divided: Joe Kent blamed Israeli pressure for the Iran war, Rep. Thomas Massie has pushed to cut aid, and Vice President JD Vance has called for changing the relationship while continuing to describe Israel as a strategic ally.

The two countries have cooperated against Iran and developed defenses against missile attacks, but their goals have not always matched during the war. A Stimson Center analysis indicates Israel sought to broaden the conflict beyond what Washington preferred. That does not establish that Israel drew the United States into a war it opposed. It does show how cooperation can leave Washington managing military costs even when its preferred limits differ from Israel’s.

The next agreement will help determine whether the alliance continues to rely on direct grants or shifts toward joint weapons development and production. Either way, the military and intelligence cooperation described in the report comes with commitments of U.S. money and weapons — and leaves Washington weighing those costs against the advantages it expects the alliance to deliver.

SolarEdge unveils U.S.-made optimizer for C&I solar

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SolarEdge’s new Duo Power Optimizer promises to simplify commercial and industrial solar installations with 50% fewer optimizer units, independent module-level power tracking, and enhanced safety features.
  • According to recent reports, the commercial and industrial (C&I) solar market is getting a latest hardware option aimed at making installations simpler without sacrificing system performance.
  • Revealed November 16 ahead of RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, the upcoming product introduces a 2:1 architecture that allows one optimizer to connect two solar modules.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SolarEdge’s new Duo Power Optimizer promises to simplify commercial and industrial solar installations with 50% fewer optimizer units, independent module-level power tracking, and enhanced safety features.

According to recent reports, the commercial and industrial (C&I) solar market is getting a latest hardware option aimed at making installations simpler without sacrificing system performance. SolarEdge Technologies has unveiled its new Duo Power Optimizer, a U.S.-manufactured solution designed to deliver module-level energy harvesting and monitoring while cutting the number of power optimizers in half.

Revealed November 16 ahead of RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, the upcoming product introduces a 2:1 architecture that allows one optimizer to connect two solar modules. Notably, each module retains its own independent maximum power point tracker (MPPT), which preserves the module-level performance benefits associated with the traditional one-to-one optimizer configurations.

For developers, EPCs and installers managing large-scale rooftop and distributed generation projects, the value here lies in fewer components to purchase, wire and install, with no trade-off in module-level optimization.

Simplifying installation without sacrificing performance.

SolarEdge’s optimization tech addresses the challenge of conventional string inverter systems, which is that an underperforming module can affect the output of an entire string. But by allowing each module to operate independently, the system limits the impact of shading, degradation or performance differences between panels.

In a recent development, the Duo brings demonstrates that capability in a two-module configuration. By reducing the number of optimizers by 50% compared with one-to-one designs, SolarEdge is targeting an opportunity to streamline balance-of-system requirements and reduce the installation labor.

Sources indicate that solarEdge’s U.S.-made Duo Power Optimizer connects two solar modules while maintaining independent module-level power tracking for commercial and industrial solar installations. Credit: SolarEdge.

It has been revealed that the hardware also incorporates design changes intended to improve jobsite efficiency. Each optimizer features two input pairs: a shorter connection for the nearest module and a pre-extended connection for the adjacent module. The arrangement reduces excess wiring and eliminates the need for field-made jumpers.

The configuration also accommodates modules with different orientations, making it particularly relevant for east-west and dual-tilt racking applications.

Safety moves closer to the module.

Beyond installation efficiency, SolarEdge is emphasizing electrical safety as a central feature of the upcoming product.

The Duo extends the organization’s Sense Connect technology to its input and output connectors, monitoring connector temperatures to identify developing complications before they potentially escalate into overheating or electrical arcs.

Industry observers note that also, the optimizer introduces what SolarEdge describes as an industry-first approach to arc fault detection: every optimizer acts as an individual arc sensor. Rather than relying exclusively on detection at the inverter, the system distributes monitoring throughout the array, allowing potential arc faults to be identified closer to their source.

Industry observers note that solarEdge says the technology provides coverage across strings with up to 3,280 feet of total cable length between the inverter and optimizer. It can also help pinpoint problems to the optimizer area, potentially making troubleshooting and maintenance more efficient.

Manufactured at SolarEdge’s Florida facility, the Duo is designed to meet U.S. Domestic Content and Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements, according to the tech giant. SolarEdge says its domestic-content eligibility levels are consistent with those of its previous U.S.-manufactured power optimizers, subject to applicable tax guidance and project-specific requirements.

A practical play for the C&I market.

For SolarEdge, the Duo represents an effort to combine three priorities that are becoming more and more key in commercial solar: installation efficiency, system-level safety, and domestic manufacturing.

Industry observers note that the technology does not fundamentally change the value proposition of module-level optimization. Instead, it looks to make that architecture more economical and easier to deploy at scale.

SolarEdge will showcase the Duo Power Optimizer at RE+ 2026.

Breaking: Medicare looks a bit different in 2027, so don't miss open enrollment

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1242 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Npr

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A counselor, right, helps a client through the Medicare signup process at a resource center for older adults in Sunrise, Florida.
  • Industry observers note that annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people.
  • It has been revealed that open enrollment runs through Dec.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A counselor, right, helps a client through the Medicare signup process at a resource center for older adults in Sunrise, Florida. Medicare open enrollment season started Oct. 15 and ends Dec. 7. Joe Cavaretta/South Florida Sun Sentinel/Tribune News Service via Getty Images hide caption.

Industry observers note that annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people. The coverage choices are complex and often consequential.

It has been revealed that open enrollment runs through Dec. 7. The strategy you choose takes effect on Jan. 1, for the full calendar year.

Industry observers note that medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn't one initiative. It's more like a build-your-own-insurance menu.

It has been revealed that roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the strategy covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there's no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn't cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services.

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

It has been revealed that as a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D, the prescription drug strategy. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.

This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care intends known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums.

"People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs," said David Lipschutz, a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.

Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage prepares send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It's a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can't find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy.

Industry observers note that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projects that the average Part D premium will increase less than $1 a month for a standalone prescription drug initiative, describing the market as stable. But that average doesn't tell the whole story. An analysis by KFF, the health policy research nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, found that enrollees who stay in their prescription drug plan will see a 50% increase on average, from $34 to $51. About 10.4 million people could pay higher premiums, not including higher deductibles and coinsurance costs.

About 4 million people are in Medicare Advantage looks that won't be offered in 2027. If they do nothing, they'll be automatically enrolled in traditional Medicare. Jenny Kane/AP hide caption.

Some beneficiaries who didn't have to pay monthly premiums in recent years will begin paying for prescription drug Part D coverage in 2027. While that change follows the 2025 introduction of federal caps on out-of-pocket drug expenses, it comes as the Trump administration is ending temporary federal subsidies that helped keep premiums down. The cap on out-of-pocket expenses for prescription drugs in 2027 will be $2,400, a total enrollees can opt tospread out over the course of the year.

Juliette Cubanski, who directs the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, stated people who don't shop around could be leaving money on the table.

"It is worth it to avoid any unpleasant surprises in the form of either higher premiums or higher cost sharing for covered services in 2027," she mentioned.

An estimated 4.3 million people now have to look for a upcoming Medicare Advantage or prescription drug plan after private insurers left the market. Those who want to stay in Medicare Advantage must select new coverage, or they'll be moved to traditional Medicare automatically. For those shopping for a new plan, low monthly premiums may be appealing, but it's important to read the fine print and add up the other costs.

"There are going to be, often, increases in cost sharing and copays, increases in out-of-pocket caps, and reductions in the scope of some of the extra benefits that Medicare Advantage aims provide," Lipschutz remarked.

Sources indicate that so ask: Is my prescription covered? Is my pharmacy preferred? Is my doctor in-network? What does the dental benefit actually cover?

And pay attention to the out-of-pocket maximum for the Advantage looks, Cubanski noted, so you know how much you might have to shell out in 2027.

"Look at that dollar value specifically," she noted.

Industry observers note that when selecting a drug proposal, enrollees must also tell their insurer how they want to pay, either by getting a bill in the mail or by having the cost deducted from their Social Security. If you don't pick a payment plan, you could get dropped from coverage.

If enrollees elect to leave their Medicare Advantage intends for traditional Medicare within their first year of joining Medicare, they have a guaranteed right to buy a Medigap proposal, with no health screening. After that, all bets are off: Insurers in most states can turn enrollees down or charge more because of a health condition. Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, and Upcoming York are exceptions.

Enrollees whose Advantage plans have not been renewed — and haven't been consolidated into another plan — can switch to traditional Medicare and buy a Medigap policy without a health screening, but they need to act before March.

Medicare experts advise enrollees to write down all their prescription drugs, as well as any procedures planned in the next year, such as a joint replacement or dental work, to help them decide which plan will cover their needs. Call a favorite doctor's office to see whether they are in-network for the aims being considered. Remember that brokers might earn commissions, especially on Advantage plans, and might not represent every plan.

Industry observers note that for unbiased help, every state has a federally funded State Health Insurance Assistance Program that offers free initiative counseling specific to your situation, in person and over the phone. To get help, go to the website at shiphelp.org/open-enrollment, email info@shiphelp.org, or call the SHIP National Technical Assistance Center at 877-839-2675.

A SHIP counselor can also help enrollees apply for benefits that help pay for Medicare premiums and prescription drug costs, such as the Medicare Savings Programs and Medicare Part D Extra Help.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

Sources indicate that NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

  • President Donald Trump will participate in the annual Turkey Pardon on Tuesday, and the West Virginia turkey farmer responsible for raising this year's two birds helps walk Fox News Digital through the process from hatch to White House ahead of the light-hearted event.
  • "We spent a little bit more one-on-one time with each of these birds to get them trained to loud noises, a lot of people present, flashing lights — just being handled — so when they get to the president, hopefully they'll act like they have some sense," Scott Rightsell told Fox News Digital about raising the birds for Tuesday's National Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turkey farmer Scott Rightsell and National Turkey Federation head Christy Puffenbarger explain the lifecycle of the turkeys receiving a presidential pardon on Tuesday.

President Donald Trump will participate in the annual Turkey Pardon on Tuesday, and the West Virginia turkey farmer responsible for raising this year's two birds helps walk Fox News Digital through the process from hatch to White House ahead of the light-hearted event.

"We spent a little bit more one-on-one time with each of these birds to get them trained to loud noises, a lot of people present, flashing lights — just being handled — so when they get to the president, hopefully they'll act like they have some sense," Scott Rightsell told Fox News Digital about raising the birds for Tuesday's National Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon.

Recent findings suggest that rightsell, who owns and operates Deans Gap Farm in rural Fort Seybert, West Virginia, with his wife Becky, found out during the summer that he would raise the turkeys for the ceremony. He received the young turkeys, called poults, in July — shortly after the celebration for America 250.

The turkeys were named Freedom and Feathers through a White House public opinion poll, beating out the options for Commander and Chief or Honey and Ham.

Freedom and Feathers, the two turkeys chosen for the 2026 Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon at the White House, on a farm where they were raised in West Virginia. (National Turkey Federation).

TRUMP'S THANKSGIVING TURKEYS ARRIVE AT LUXURY DC HOTEL AS AMERICANS VOTE ON THEIR NAMES.

Sources indicate that "We've had them from the middle of the July until now," noted Rightsell. "The turkeys weigh probably 40 to 45 pounds right now.".

He added that besides the aforementioned training, the birds receive the same treatment as all the others that he raises on the farm, which he and his wife founded in 2015.

"Being on national TV, that's a massive deal," Rightsell stated when asked what he was looking forward to most about his trip to the nation's capital this week.

"I mean That's probably what we're looking forward to the most is being on national TV, actually meeting the president, which everybody does not get to do that. And getting to converse with him and the first lady, that's gonna be a real treat for us.".

From left to right, Becky Rightsell, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, Scott Rightsell, Gov. Patrick Morrisey, R-W.Va., and Christy Puffenbarger pose for a photo in West Virginia. (National Turkey Federation).

The National Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon has been a tradition for 79 years, recurring annually since President Harry Truman occupied the White House, according to Christy Puffenbarger.

Sources indicate that puffenbarger is this year's National Turkey Federation chairwoman, a position that rotates annually. She's the first woman to hold the role.

In a recent development, typically, the pardon event is held in the Rose Garden. However, Trump will host the pardoning on the latest South Lawn helipad Tuesday afternoon. A White House spokesperson tells Fox News Digital that Trump will deliver remarks about "how well our nation is doing" ahead of the holiday.

First lady Melania Trump, Vice President JD Vance and a litany of Cabinet secretaries, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Education Secretary Linda McMahon. Attorney General Todd Blanche will also attend. So will latest White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

It has been revealed that both turkeys receive a pardon, but which turkey participates in the pardoning ceremony depends on the American people, who vote for their preferred bird on the White House's website. Voters are still deciding Tuesday morning which fleshy fowl will be pardoned later today.

INSIDE THE THANKSGIVING TURKEY HOTLINE THAT'S BEEN SAVING HOLIDAY DINNERS FOR 45 YEARS.

Recent findings suggest that neither bird will end up on anyone's Thanksgiving dinner table. The turkey that doesn't receive a pardon remains behind the scenes at the White House, "for moral support," as Puffenbarger put it. If the chosen bird gets stage fright or cannot carry out the ceremonial duties, the second bird is on standby.

Freedom and Feathers, the two turkeys chosen for the 2026 Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon at the White House, on a farm where they were raised in West Virginia. (National Turkey Federation).

It has been revealed that "What I'm really looking forward to, obviously, like Scott and Becky, is meeting the president and his wife and representing this industry, and really [I] would like to thank the president for continuing this tradition," Puffenbarger told Fox News Digital. "Because I do think it is a very nice event. It showcases not only our industry, but the tradition of turkey at Thanksgiving.".

Puffenbarger indicates the industry as a whole will provide 30 million pounds of turkey to Americans enjoying the Thanksgiving holiday this year.

"And to be able to showcase it at a positive, fun event like that ... it'll be quite an honor for myself and my family," she mentioned.

After spending their first few months of life like any normal turkey, the royal treatment for Feathers and Freedom began on Thursday.

They left for Washington, D.C., after a star-studded send-off from a local elementary school in Brandywine, West Virginia, where Becky Rightsell is also a teacher.

Secretary Rollins attended the sendoff, as did West Virginia Governor Patrick Morrisey.

Recent findings suggest that "It’s so humbling for West Virginia to be named to have two of the turkeys that get pardoned. This is history in the making, only the second time that’s happened," Morrisey told WDTV during the ceremony.

According to recent reports, freedom and Feathers, the two turkeys chosen for the 2026 Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon at the White House, walk on a red carpet at the Willard Intercontinental Hotel in Washington, D.C. (Department of Agriculture).

BROOKE ROLLINS, MONICA CROWLEY: AMERICA’S FAMILY FARMS HAVE KEPT US STRONG FOR 250 YEARS.

Sunday night, the birds arrived at the five-star Willard InterContinental Hotel in Washington, D.C., where they received "presidential treatment," according to the Department of Agriculture (USDA), which posted photos of the turkeys sitting on the beds in a hotel room.

It has been revealed that A red carpet was rolled out as they strolled through the lobby of the hotel to much fanfare. Once in the room, the birds were greeted by a layer of crunchy fall leaves lining the floor.

But the fun doesn't end after Tuesday's pardoning. Instead, the turkeys will be whisked away for their next adventure.

"Immediately afterwards, another cool thing, these birds will get on an airplane and fly to beautiful College Station, Texas, where they will retire to live out the rest of their lives at Texas A&M University," Puffenbarger explained.

Freedom and Feathers, the two turkeys chosen for the 2026 Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon at the White House, sit on beds at the Willard Intercontinental Hotel in Washington, D.C. (Department of Agriculture).

Friday night, Texas A&M's football team is scheduled to host rival Texas, the fifth-ranked college football team in the country.

Feathers and Freedom will be the guests of honor at the game.

"I don't know how much they know about football, but I feel sure they will have a good time," Puffenbarger said.

  • American Military Project director Will Thibeau reacts to the federal approval of a controlled detonation of expired explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.
  • Army will detonate 68 barrels of unstable, degraded bomb-making chemicals in Iowa on Wednesday morning after a federal appeals court rejected a legal challenge and allowed the controlled blast to move forward.
  • In a statement late Monday, Army officials confirmed they are proceeding with destroying the crystallized lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown in coordination with state, local and federal authorities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American Military Project director Will Thibeau reacts to the federal approval of a controlled detonation of expired explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Thibeau also breaks down a Wall Street Journal report indicating the U.S. suspects Iran is behind dozens of recent cyberattacks targeting commercial ships in the Middle East.

The U.S. Army will detonate 68 barrels of unstable, degraded bomb-making chemicals in Iowa on Wednesday morning after a federal appeals court rejected a legal challenge and allowed the controlled blast to move forward.

In a statement late Monday, Army officials confirmed they are proceeding with destroying the crystallized lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown in coordination with state, local and federal authorities.

It has been revealed that "This is a consensus decision," Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle posted on social media. "Every expert agency agrees, and both Iowa’s current and incoming Governors say the call belongs to the experts.".

FEDERAL APPEALS COURT CLEARS ARMY TO DETONATE VOLATILE IOWA EXPLOSIVES AS DEM GOV-ELECT REFUSES TO SIGN OFF.

In a recent development, A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Nov. 19, 2026 in Middletown, Iowa. (Scott Olson/Getty Images).

Hours earlier, a three-judge panel of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals lifted a temporary pause and denied an emergency request from the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club to block the operation. The judges found that the Environmental Protection Agency built adequate safeguards into its emergency permit to limit lead dust dispersal.

"Here we are faced with a situation in which the risk is between a controlled detonation and an unplanned explosion, not between the risk of a controlled detonation and no explosion at all," the court wrote.

Industry observers note that the ruling followed a Truth Social post from President Donald Trump declaring he had ordered the military to hold off unless both the appeals court and Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand signed off. Trump warned he would hold Sand "responsible for any and all death or destruction" if the operation were blocked.

Sand, who takes office in January, declined to approve or reject the blast on Monday evening. He posted on X that the Trump administration should make the call based on the experts it brought in months ago and urged federal officials to release their briefing details publicly.

DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT.

Meanwhile, a flight carrying Army officials departed Joint Base Andrews for Iowa just before Trump's post went live.

Industry observers note that the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. (U.S. Army via AP).

It has been revealed that the operation has already been postponed three times amid public concern over toxic lead dust. Munitions specialists warned in court filings that dropping temperatures increase the risk that crystallized material inside the barrels could trigger an accidental, fatal explosion if left untreated.

In a public advisory, the Army noted Wednesday's blast will produce two rapid detonations, ground vibrations and a dust plume expected to linger for no more than an hour.

Sources indicate that an aerial view highlights homes on Nov. 20, 2026 in Middletown, Iowa. (Scott Olson/Getty Images).

People living near Middletown, some of whom have already sealed their windows and doors, have been advised to stay indoors and wash outdoor surfaces with water afterward.

The Pentagon chief "overindulged in ego, in attitude, and in entitlement," Kasper stated, according to the report.

In a recent development, leapmotor just produced its 2 millionth vehicle, all EVs of course. The EV startup has seen a meteoric rise in the highly competitive Chinese EV market, and increasingly abroad. Of course, most of us in the US and even in Europe know nothing or next to nothing about Leapmotor, but it has clearly been more effective than hundreds or even thousands of other companies that have tried to launch and scale up EV production.

One interesting thing to note regarding this milestone: it’s peanuts compared to Leapmotor’s aims for the next few years. In 2026 alone, Leapmotor plans to produce one million vehicles, and it’s on track to do so. That means that, this year, the organization plans to produce as many vehicles as half of Leapmotor’s cumulative total at the moment. So, it will just be sometime in the middle of next year that the company will reach 3 million cumulative EVs produced.

The firm is now producing more than 100,000 vehicles a month — for four months running.

Industry observers note that naturally, the company’s plan is to keep growing. As part of that effort, it just released a latest model, the Lafa 5 compact hatchback, with pre-sales starting earlier today. Also, another new model, the D19 SUV, just had its 50,000th unit produced.

In a recent development, so, yes, keep an eye on Leapmotor. It’s already a wildly successful young EV manufacturer, and it looks like it is going to continue growing fast.
